knownFor: Priest and then bishop of Jerusalem, whose lectures to the people preparing for baptism survive, and who was driven from his see three times.
datesNote: Born about 315 or a few years before, by Gifford's reckoning; bishop from about 350; died 386, by Gifford's reckoning from Jerome's eight years under Theodosius

keyWorks.title: Procatechesis and Catechetical Lectures 1 to 18
keyWorks.about: given in Lent, in 348 by Gifford's date, to those to be baptized at Easter, going through the creed of Jerusalem clause by clause

keyWorks.title: Mystagogic Lectures 1 to 5

traces: Gifford's chapters on the lectures draw from them the order of baptism, the anointing and the Eucharist as they were kept at Jerusalem.
Theodoret of Cyrus, in his Dialogues, cites the fourth lecture as a testimony of Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem.

Egeria, a pilgrim from the West, wrote home to the women of her community about the teaching of the candidates at Jerusalem: the bishop's chair in the great church, with the candidates sitting around him and their fathers and mothers standing by; the Scriptures taught from Genesis through the forty days; the creed taught after five weeks; and in Easter week the bishop explaining the rites in the cave of the Anastasis, with the doors shut. She never names the bishop.

Jerome, writing against John of Jerusalem in 397 or 398, says it was their custom to give public lectures for forty days to those to be baptized, and speaks of what John was accustomed to give the candidates in church through Lent.
Jerome lists Cyril's catechetical lectures in Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 112, which Gifford says was written about six years after Cyril's death.

A note at the end of the Procatechesis lets copies be lent to those preparing for baptism and to the baptized, and says they are not to be given to catechumens or to anyone who is not a Christian. Gifford says it is doubtful whether Cyril or a later editor wrote it.
remembered: Jerome of Strido calls him "bishop of Jerusalem often expelled by the church, and at last received."
The bishops at Constantinople in 382 wrote that he "has in several places fought a good fight against the Arians."
Gifford quotes the Roman Martyrology, which keeps his day on 18 March.

uncertain: Socrates of Constantinople and Sozomen, a church historian of the fifth century, say the party of Acacius of Caesarea pushed out Maximus and put Cyril in his place. Jerome of Strido, hostile to Cyril, says in his Chronicle, as Gifford quotes it, that Cyril gave up the priesthood Maximus had given him to be made bishop by the Arians, and that he later pushed aside Heraclius, whom Maximus had named. The bishops at Constantinople in 382 wrote that Cyril was canonically ordained by the bishops of the province. Gifford, who defends Cyril, calls the accounts of Socrates and Jerome "irreconcileable, and both improbable", and follows Reischl's suggestion that Cyril was named in Maximus's lifetime and ordained in due form. Gifford notes that Jerome and Cyril took opposite sides in the split at Antioch.

Sozomen, who says he looked into why Acacius deposed him, gives the sale of the church's veil and ornaments in a famine, and calls it a pretext. Socrates says he could not learn the charges, and that Cyril stayed away for two years "owing to fear." Theodoret of Cyrus says Acacius "seized some small occasion." Theodoret also gives Acacius's later tale of a gold-threaded robe sold to a dancer, who fell and died.

Socrates says that in 381 Cyril accepted the word homoousion, "having retracted his former opinion." Sozomen says he had once followed Macedonius. Gifford, following Touttée, the Benedictine editor, rejects both, since the lectures teach the Son's unity of essence with the Father without the word.

Some manuscripts name John, Cyril's successor, as the author of the Mystagogic Lectures. Gifford, with Touttée, holds that all the lectures are Cyril's, since the eighteenth lecture promises the later ones and they match it.

Socrates says that when Julian let the Jews begin to rebuild the Temple, Cyril foretold that one stone would not be left upon another, and an earthquake followed that night. Gifford thinks Cyril may well have expected the attempt to fail, but finds "no satisfactory evidence that he ventured to foretell any miraculous interposition."
The dates of his exiles are reckoned by Gifford, about 357, 360 and about 367. The names of the men set in his place differ between the witnesses.

Gifford dates the letter on the cross to 7 May 351, from the letter itself, which is not held in the Library. Gifford reports a doubt over the word "Consubstantial" in its last prayer, and holds the letter as a whole genuine.

No source used here gives his birth, parents or schooling. Gifford names one relative, his sister's son Gelasius, whom Cyril made bishop of Caesarea. Gifford reckons his birth from what Cyril seems to have seen of the holy places as a boy.

Taken down as spoken. The only statement that hearers took the lectures down is a note added at the end of the eighteenth lecture in the older of the Munich manuscripts. It says these lectures alone were taken down when spoken, by some of the earnest students, in a year it counts as 352 and equates with 360 of our era. Gifford says the lectures cannot be so late. The note's author is not known. The title of the first lecture in the manuscripts says only that it was delivered extempore.

Egeria never names the bishop whose teaching she describes. Her name and her date are reconstructed by modern scholars. Her editors, following Férotin, place her visit toward the end of the fourth century, in the reign of Theodosius, so the bishop may have been Cyril or his successor John; Karl Meister argued in 1909 for about 534. The editors say her descriptions tally in most respects with Cyril's lectures, but they date the lectures to 386.
Socrates says Cyril was the first and indeed the only clergyman to appeal against his deposition in the way commonly done in the secular courts.

Theodoret says that after Acacius deposed him Cyril went by way of Antioch to Tarsus, where the bishop Silvanus, whose people greatly enjoyed the stranger's teaching, refused to stop him from taking part in the church's services, though Acacius had written to tell him of the deposition. Theodoret also says that at Seleucia Acacius refused to sit in council with Cyril as a man stripped of his bishopric, and that when Cyril would not withdraw Acacius left.
Sozomen says that when Theodosius was raised to the throne all the churches of the East except Jerusalem's were in the hands of the Arians.

Rufinus of Aquileia, in his Latin Church History, says that Cyril took up the bishop's office after Maximus when the ordination was already confused, and that he wavered sometimes in faith and more often in communion.

The men set in Cyril's place. Socrates gives Arrenius, then Heraclius, then Hilary; Sozomen gives Erennius, Heraclius and Hilarius; Jerome's Chronicle sets Eutychius, Hireneus and Hilarius between four tenures of Cyril. Epiphanius, Cyril's contemporary, says that a party was split into rival groups because Cyril and Eutychius bore anger against each other, and he places Cyril with Basil the Galatian, Anianus of Antioch and George of Laodicea.

The third removal rests on Gifford. He dates it probably to 367 and bases it on an order of Valens, which he quotes from Sozomen, that bishops banished under Constantius and back in office under Julian be ejected; Gifford applies this to Cyril, of whose third banishment he says no particulars are known.

Later readers and editions are known here only through Gifford. He lists Gelasius of Rome and Leontius of Byzantium as quoting the fourth lecture, and Theophanes as defending Cyril's orthodoxy on the ground that he avoided the word of one being, which then offended most people, and taught the same doctrine in other words. He reports a Slavonic version put into Polish before 1560, John Grodecq's Latin version of 1564 with a preface dated at Trent in 1563, and an Armenian version printed at Vienna in 1832. In the seventeenth century two French Protestant theologians attacked the Easter-week lectures on doctrinal grounds, with more zeal than success in Gifford's judgment, and Touttée defended them. None of those texts is held here.

briefReferences: Catechetical Lecture 13, section 23, tr. Gifford: the hearers' shout of praise at Golgotha, and the warning that follows not to take the faith back when persecution comes. Gifford's note gives the Greek of the two sentences about the shout.

Gifford's introduction: the lectures were given in the great church that Constantine built at the site of the tomb, consecrated in 335, and the Easter-week lectures in the small chapel that held the tomb.

Gifford, after Touttée: the Lent of the lectures was that of 348, and they follow the creed of Jerusalem article by article. Catechetical Lecture 18, section 33, promises the Easter-week lectures in the Holy Place of the Resurrection.
The note at the end of Catechetical Lecture 18, from the older Munich manuscript, that the lectures were taken down when spoken, and Gifford's reply on its date.
Procatechesis 5: the man who came to court a woman, and Jesus angling for him. Procatechesis 12: tell nothing to those outside.
Catechetical Lecture 5, section 12: the creed in a few lines, since not all can read the Scriptures, to be learned by heart and not written on paper.

Catechetical Lecture 13, sections 4 and 39, and Lecture 14, section 5: Golgotha, the tomb and its stone, and the traces of the old garden, as the places he points to. The brief names Golgotha and the tomb.

Mystagogic Lecture 1, sections 1, 2, 4 and 9: waiting until after baptism, facing west and renouncing Satan with the hand stretched out, and turning east to the place of light. Mystagogic Lecture 2, section 2: the stripping. Mystagogic Lecture 5, section 21: the left hand a throne for the right at communion.
Gifford's introduction, with Touttée: the copies that name John as author of the Mystagogic Lectures, and the promises in the earlier lectures that the five fulfill.
Socrates, Church History 2.38, and Sozomen, Church History 4.20: the party of Acacius and Patrophilus ejected Maximus and put Cyril in his see.
Jerome, Chronicle, in Latin: his charge that Cyril gave up his ordination as a priest on the promise of the see from Acacius and the Arians.
The bishops' letter of 382, in Theodoret, Church History 5.9: Cyril canonically ordained by the bishops of the province, and one who has fought a good fight against the Arians in several places.

Sozomen, Church History 4.25: the dispute with Acacius over rank, the sale of the veil and sacred ornaments in a famine, and the pretext. Socrates, Church History 2.40: charges unknown to him, two years' absence owing to fear, and the appeal the emperor Constantius allowed. Gifford: the date about 357.
Socrates, Church History 2.42: the synod of Constantinople in 360. Socrates, Church History 3.1: Julian's recall of the exiled bishops. Gifford: the third removal, probably about 367.

Socrates, Church History 5.8, and Sozomen, Church History 7.7: Cyril at the council of 381 and the doubt over his earlier views. Gifford, after Touttée: the lectures teach the doctrine without the word.
Socrates, Church History 5.15: his death, and John's succession, with the editor's date of 386.
The note at the end of the Procatechesis that lets copies be lent to the baptized and to those preparing, and Gifford's doubt who wrote it. Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 112: the lectures listed.
Jerome, Against John of Jerusalem 13: the custom of forty days of public lectures to those to be baptized.

Egeria, Pilgrimage, tr. McClure and Feltoe, with Bernard's independent translation: the bishop's chair, the Scriptures, the creed after five weeks, and the Easter-week teaching in the Anastasis with the doors shut. She never names the bishop; her editors' date for her visit is the end of the fourth century.
World census, Jerusalem and Its Pilgrims: his tradition.

quotationOriginals.modern: Do you see this place, Golgotha?
quotationOriginals.printed: Thou seest this spot of Golgotha!
quotationOriginals.work: Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechetical Lecture 13, section 23, tr. Gifford, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, vol. 7
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The Greek is held only in Gifford's note in his introduction, which gives these two sentences from the lecture; the lecture itself is not held in Greek. Gifford's English ends the sentence with an exclamation mark, and the Greek he prints ends it with a question mark, which the modern wording follows.

quotationOriginals.modern: You answer with a shout of praise, as if you agree.
quotationOriginals.printed: Thou answerest with a shout of praise, as if assenting.
quotationOriginals.work: Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechetical Lecture 13, section 23, tr. Gifford, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, vol. 7
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The Greek is held only in Gifford's note, as for the sentence before it.

quotationOriginals.modern: I knew well that seeing persuades far more than hearing. So I waited for this time.
quotationOriginals.printed: since I well knew that seeing is far more persuasive than hearing, I waited for the present season
quotationOriginals.work: Cyril (or, in some copies, John), Mystagogic Lecture 1, section 1, tr. Gifford, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, vol. 7
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The Greek is not held, so the English stands alone. The modern wording makes Gifford's one sentence two. Some copies name John as author of the five Easter-week lectures; Gifford holds them Cyril's.

quotationOriginals.modern: The bishop talks through each point and sets it out. Meanwhile the voices of those applauding are so loud that they can be heard outside the church.
quotationOriginals.printed: And while the bishop discusses and sets forth each point, the voices of those who applaud are so loud that they can be heard outside the church.
quotationOriginals.work: Egeria, Pilgrimage, the Easter-week teaching, tr. M. L. McClure and C. L. Feltoe
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Egeria's Latin is not held, so the English stands alone. The independent English of J. H. Bernard (lines 11098-11101 of its file) agrees: so loud are the voices of those applauding that they are heard outside the church. She does not name the bishop.

quotationOriginals.printed: See that thou recant not in time of persecution.
